analysis.one_liner: Ends the insurance industry's federal antitrust exemption for price fixing and monopolizing markets.
analysis.headline: "The bill to end insurers' antitrust exemption for price fixing was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a vote in the two years it had left."
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, insurance companies have had a broad exemption from federal antitrust laws, the rules against price fixing and monopolies. This bill would strip that exemption for the worst practices: insurers colluding on prices, dividing up markets so they don't have to compete, forcing customers to buy policies they don't want, and trying to corner a market. Insurers could still legally share claims data and do actuarial work, so small companies would not lose the information they need to set rates. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and businesses who buy insurance. If insurers collude on prices or divide up markets today, the federal antitrust laws that apply to almost every other industry cannot touch them; this bill would let customers and the government sue insurers for those practices, just as they can sue any other cartel. People in lines of insurance where a few big companies dominate — like some health, property, and casualty markets — stand to benefit most if it leads to more competition and lower premiums.

how_it_helps.text: It amends the McCarran-Ferguson Act — the 1945 law that gave insurance companies a broad exemption from federal antitrust laws — so that price fixing by insurers would no longer be shielded from antitrust suits.

It makes three other practices subject to antitrust law: dividing up markets so insurers agree not to compete with each other, forcing customers to buy one type of insurance in order to get another, and monopolizing or attempting to monopolize any part of the insurance business.

It protects legitimate cooperation: insurers could still legally share historical claims data, calculate loss development factors, and perform actuarial services as long as those activities do not restrain trade, so small insurers can keep the information they need to price policies.

analysis.who_pays: Insurance companies that benefit from the exemption. With antitrust liability possible for price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization, insurers would face legal exposure and pressure on coordinated pricing, and could see margins squeezed in markets where they currently set prices without fear of antitrust suits.

drawbacks.text: Insurance has traditionally been regulated by the states, and industry-backed arguments hold that federal antitrust enforcement could override or clash with that state-based system of oversight.

Antitrust liability can bring legal costs and uncertainty that insurers may pass on in premiums, and some shared industry data-pooling genuinely helps small insurers price policies accurately — which is why the bill carves out exemptions for collecting historical loss data and actuarial services, with a transition period for some 'trend factor' cooperation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: consumers would be able to sue insurers that collude on prices, and the bill is carefully drafted to keep the data-sharing arrangements that small insurers legitimately need, with transition periods to soften the change. The main honest cost is legal uncertainty in a sector that states have regulated for decades, and the possibility of some compliance costs flowing into premiums — but the bill's targeted carve-outs and phase-in are designed to limit exactly that. On balance the consumer benefit of ending an industry-wide price-fixing shield outweighs the manageable transition costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 29, 2003 and referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
That referral was the only action the bill ever received; the committee never reported it, held no recorded markup or vote, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 without the bill moving.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurance companies kept the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption, which shields price-fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization in their business from federal antitrust law, and no consumer protections from those practices were enacted.

for.name: 13 of 205 House Democrats

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 29, 2003 and took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Insurance industry
against.role: Industry holding the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption
against.what_they_did: The industry has long defended the McCarran-Ferguson exemption and opposed legislation to narrow it.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 supporters were Democrats (sponsor, original co-sponsor, and 13 cosponsors); no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-controlled House never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill strips insurers of the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption for price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization, exposing those practices to federal antitrust suits. Consumers who face insurers' concerted price-setting would gain the legal remedy they currently lack.

The bill preserves the exemption for collecting and sharing historical loss data and for actuarial services, which small insurers rely on to compete with larger firms. Small insurers also get a longer transition period (4 years versus 2) before the trend-factor carve-out ends.
